explain.say: Imagine going to bed on 4 October and waking up on 15 October! That really happened in some countries in 1582. Look at the first point on the timeline. Back in 45 BCE, Julius Caesar's calendar added a leap day every four years.

explain.say: See the sun at the second point? Caesar's year was 11 minutes too long. That sounds tiny, but over many centuries the dates slipped away from the seasons. By the 1500s, the first day of spring, called the equinox, came about 10 days early. Can you see how small mistakes add up?

explain.say: Now look at October 1582. Pope Gregory the Thirteenth's new calendar fixed the drift by simply skipping ten days. Thursday 4 October was followed straight away by Friday 15 October. It also made most century years skip their leap day.

faq.a: The calendar Julius Caesar brought in, starting in 45 BCE. It had 365 days with a leap day every fourth year, which made the year a little too long.
The Julian year was about 11 minutes longer than the real year. Those minutes added up to about one day every 128 years, so the seasons slowly slipped.
asks: Why did the calendar go wrong?

faq.q: Why were ten days skipped in 1582?
faq.a: To put the spring equinox back near 21 March, where it had been in the year 325. Skipping ten days fixed the drift at once.
Britain switched in 1752, 170 years after Italy and Spain. By then the old calendar had slipped one more day, so 2 September was followed by 14 September.
asks: When did Britain change its calendar?

faq.q: Do all countries use the Gregorian calendar?
faq.a: Most countries use it for business and government, though a few, like Ethiopia, Iran and Nepal, officially use their own. Many people also keep other calendars for festivals, such as the Islamic, Hebrew, Chinese and Hindu calendars.
asks: Is the Gregorian calendar used everywhere?

facts: In 1582, Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October in countries such as Italy, Spain and Portugal.
Britain and its colonies changed to the Gregorian calendar in 1752, jumping from 2 to 14 September.
